Manslayer
măn'slā-ər
n. (one who has killed a man; in the law, the man who killed at unawares and might flee to a city of refuge)
English man with slayer. The Hebrew ratsach is the verb of the sixth commandment; the law distinguishes by intent between the murderer, who dies, and the manslayer, who flees.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The law of Israel drew a line the modern conscience often blurs. Six of the Levites' cities were set apart “for the manslayer, that he may flee thither” (Num 35:6), and the case is defined: “that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares” (Num 35:11). The refuge is not an evasion of justice but the guarantee of it: “And they shall be unto you cities for refuge from the avenger; that the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment” (Num 35:12). He must be tried. If the killing was with hatred, he dies; if at unawares, he lives, but not freely — “he shall abide in it unto the death of the high priest, which was anointed with the holy oil” (Num 35:25). Blood has been shed and the land is not clean until a death occurs; the death that releases him is the high priest's. The type is not accidental. The man who has taken a life and cannot go home is set at liberty by the death of an anointed priest — and the New Testament names the High Priest whose death opens every gate.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a manslayer as one that has slain a human being; and manslaughter, in law, as the unlawful killing of a man without malice, express or implied — distinguished from murder.

expand to see more

MANSLAYER, n. One that has slain a human being.

MANSLAUGHTER, n. In law, the unlawful killing of a man without malice, express or implied.

This may be voluntary, upon a sudden heat, or involuntary, in the commission of an unlawful act.

Cities for refuge… for the manslayer. Num. xxxv.

Key Scripture

Num 35:11 — "Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares."

Num 35:12 — "And they shall be unto you cities for refuge from the avenger; that the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment."

Num 35:25 — "And the congregation shall deliver the slayer out of the hand of the revenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to the city of his refuge, whither he was fled: and he shall abide in it unto the death of the high priest, which was anointed with the holy oil."

Rev 15:2 — "And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God."

Modern Corruption

Intent has been made either everything or nothing in modern thinking about killing, while the law of refuge weighs intent carefully and still requires a death before the land is clean.

expand to see more

The cities of refuge answer two errors at once. The first collapses all killing into one category, so that any taking of life is murder and no distinction of intent is allowed; the law refuses this, providing a road, a city and a trial for the man who killed at unawares, and Deuteronomy adds the case of the axe head flying from the helve. The second error is the reverse, and it is the more common now: intent is made the whole matter, so that a man who did not mean it is held to owe nothing at all. The law refuses that too. The manslayer is not acquitted and sent home; he leaves his house, his fields and his standing, and lives in a city not his own until the high priest dies. Guilt and liability are not identical, and Scripture keeps both. A life has been ended, and the accounting does not vanish because the heart was innocent of malice.

The release is what makes the statute gospel rather than mere jurisprudence. The manslayer's term is not fixed by years or by good behaviour; it ends at the death of the high priest, and at no other event. He waits for a death he did not cause and cannot hasten, and that death sets him free to return to the land of his possession. Hebrews takes up the whole apparatus — a High Priest anointed not with oil but by the Spirit, who entered once into the holy place having obtained eternal redemption — and the epistle even uses the figure of fleeing for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us. The city gate stood open and the roads were kept clear by law so that no man's flight should fail for want of a way. That is how the gospel is to be preached: plainly enough that a man running for his life can find it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ratsach (H7523), to slay or murder — the verb of the sixth commandment, used both of the murderer and of the manslayer; with miqlat (H4733), a refuge, and goel haddam, the avenger of blood.

expand to see more

Hebrew ratsach (H7523) — to slay; thou shalt not kill, and the slayer that killeth at unawares; Exodus 20:13, Numbers 35:11.

Hebrew miqlat (H4733) — a refuge, an asylum; the six cities appointed among the Levites; Numbers 35:6.

Hebrew goel (H1350) — a redeemer, a kinsman; here the avenger of blood, the same word as kinsman-redeemer; Numbers 35:12.

Hebrew bishgagah — at unawares, by error; the phrase that divides manslaughter from murder; Numbers 35:11.

Greek archiereus (G749) — high priest; whose death released the manslayer, and whose antitype released the guilty; Hebrews 9:11.

Usage

"“That the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment” — refuge as the guarantee of trial."

"“Which killeth any person at unawares” — intent weighed, and liability kept."

"“Unto the death of the high priest” — a release no prisoner could hasten."
